extracted.intended_audience: employers, occupational-safety professionals, public commenters, and other stakeholders evaluating or implementing OSHA's proposed heat standard
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evidence summary from OSHA's NPRM describing controls, measurement endpoints, and study-evidence considerations for preventing heat-related illness in workplaces; intended to inform rulemaking comments, employer implementation, and regulatory evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydration and nutrition
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining hydration is important for maintaining cognitive and physical performance; interventions include hydration, electrolytes, and access to cool, potable water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and specifics: access and availability to cool, potable water; training on hydration; addressing availability of fluids during rest breaks in the prevention plan. Morris et al. (2020) and Racinais et al. (2015) note drinking sufficient fluids before and after work/exercise. Guidance implies employers should provide potable water, make it accessible during rest breaks, and include hydration training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental conditioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify the work environment to reduce heat exposure (e.g., fans, shade, air-conditioning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit examples: fans, shade, air-conditioning. Two expert groups recommended air conditioning. Use environment-based work modifications (e.g., number of rest breaks) informed by measured conditions. Note: fans recommended at temperatures below 40 °C (104 °F) in some guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimal clothing / Textiles and PPE
rubrics_metrics.description: Use clothing and PPE that promotes heat dissipation while protecting against hazards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hats; loose fitting, light/brightly colored/reflective, breathable clothing; ventilation patches in PPE; cooling garments/PPE; thin, lightweight materials that promote heat dissipation; PPE that fits properly; ventilated openings; removal of PPE/extra layers during rest periods. Employers should balance protection from work hazards with heat dissipation needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological adaptation (acclimatization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement acclimatization programs to reduce physiological heat strain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example plan: a 5–7 day acclimatization plan tailored for new and returning workers and adjusted for environmental conditions and PPE; include training on benefits of acclimatization. Racinais et al. and Morrissey et al. emphasize repeated heat exposure (e.g., ≥60 minutes/day for 1–2 weeks for athletes) as effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing / administrative controls (work-rest cycles and rest breaks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use administrative controls such as scheduled rest breaks and adjusted work schedules to reduce metabolic heat generation and cumulative heat strain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length and frequency of breaks should be adjusted based on heat exposure, workload, acclimatization, and clothing/PPE. Rest breaks allow hydration, PPE removal, and use of shaded/cooled/fanned areas. Evidence shows longer breaks are generally more effective than shorter breaks. Studies provide example ratios and schedules (e.g., 3:1, 1:1, 1:3 work/rest ratios; 10‑minute breaks added to produce reduced %HRmax in some field studies). Modeling studies suggest break timing (e.g., 15-minute break after 120 minutes at certain WBGTs) to balance productivity and protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal cooling options / body cooling methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide personal and local cooling strategies to reduce heat storage and physiological strain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include cold water ingestion, water immersion, iced garments/towels, cooling vests, ice, portable cooling strategies in areas without electricity, and cooling during rest breaks. Guidance notes using cooling before, during, and after work and use of cooling PPE under other PPE when PPE cannot be removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency procedures and plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Have site-specific emergency plans and identified personnel for implementation and management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements: availability of an emergency plan for each work site; identification of personnel to create, manage, and implement the plan; make the plan available, rehearse it, and review it annually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor worker physiological indicators (e.g., heart rate, body/core temperature) to identify heat strain and guide interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: checking heart rate and body temperature. OSHA and expert groups consider physiological monitoring (e.g., core body temperature, heart rate, rectal temperature, HRV, physiological strain index, %HRmax) as informative intermediary endpoints to assess risk and effectiveness of controls. Monitoring may inform rest timing and emergency response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat hygiene, training, and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide annual, accessible training and communication on heat-related illness prevention and response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: annual training on heat-related illness, prevention, first aid, and emergency response in language and manner easily understood; designated personnel or buddy systems to monitor symptoms; communication strategies to inform employees of mitigation strategies before shifts; use of occupational health exam results to educate employees when exams occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental monitoring and measurement practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure environmental heat exposures close to work sites and consider multiple environmental factors in assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: measure conditions as close to the work site as possible; consider temperature, humidity, wind speed, radiance, work demands, PPE, and worker acclimatization status when assessing heat stress. Use monitoring data to include environment-based work modifications (e.g., adjust number/duration of rest breaks) in the prevention plan. WBGT and heat index are referenced in studies as exposure metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of intermediary endpoints and outcome measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate interventions using intermediary physiological endpoints that are on the path to heat-related illness (HRIs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermediary metrics cited include core body temperature, rectal temperature, heart rate, %HRmax, physiological strain index, heart rate variability (HRV), skin temperature, time-to-exhaustion, and modeled estimates of core temperature. OSHA accepts studies that use these metrics as informative evidence of risk reduction even when clinical HRI outcomes are not observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shade (solar radiation exposure reduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide shade for work or rest to reduce exposure to solar radiation and overall heat load.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies show shade reduces skin temperature, improves thermal sensation, and can improve endurance/work output. Rest breaks taken in shaded areas are generally more protective than breaks taken in sun; however shaded, non-air-conditioned rest breaks may be insufficient for high-exertion tasks per some observational findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work-rest ratio specification and WBGT-informed scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specified work-rest ratios and WBGT thresholds to set allowable continuous work durations and break timings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental studies examined specific ratios (e.g., continuous work, 3:1, 1:1, 1:3) at particular WBGTs and found longer rest ratios generally reduced instances of rectal temperature exceeding 38 °C. Modeling (e.g., Monte Carlo) suggested specific break timings (e.g., 15-minute break after 120 minutes at 28.9 °C WBGT) to maximize productivity while protecting health. Employers should consider WBGT and metabolic rate when choosing ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence quality, external validity, and study limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the relevance and limitations of studies used to justify controls, including differences between laboratory and real-world occupational settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA notes laboratory experimental studies have controlled conditions enabling precise measurement but may lack generalizability to workplace settings; some studies simulated work tasks to increase applicability. Limitations cited include small sample sizes, healthy/selected participants (e.g., screened firefighters), fixed work rates that prevent self-pacing, not providing water in studies, and varying baseline conditions across comparison periods. Commenters should consider these factors when weighing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment structure and work incentives as risk modifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that pay systems and economic incentives (e.g., piece-rate pay) can influence exertion and break-taking, thereby affecting HRI risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational evidence cited increased odds of HRI in piece-rate workers versus hourly-paid workers, likely due to incentives to work harder and reduce breaks. Policy and prevention plans should consider economic and organizational incentives that may discourage use of breaks or mitigation measures.
